props.title: Baby Blood

sections.content: Baby Blood (1990) stands as a grotesque milestone in French body horror, following the disturbing journey of a circus performer possessed by an ancient parasitic entity compelling her to kill. Director Alain Robak channels both David Cronenberg's visceral transformations and Roman Polanski's psychological horror, particularly Rosemary's Baby (1968). The film's unflinching violence and dark humor established a distinctive voice in European horror that influenced later works like Inside (2007) and Raw (2016).

sections.content: The parasitic horror subgenre gained significant traction in French extremity cinema following Baby Blood. Films like Martyrs (2008) and High Tension (2003) continued exploring bodily invasion and feminine rage through increasingly brutal lenses. The film's emphasis on pregnancy horror particularly resonates with Grace (2009) and Prevenge (2016), both examining motherhood through a horror lens.

Baby Blood's influence extends beyond pure horror into arthouse territory. The film's blend of body horror and dark comedy can be traced in later works like Julia Ducournau's Raw (2016) and Titane (2021), which similarly explore body transformation and primal urges through a distinctly French lens. SUBHEAD: Evolution of Body Horror

While American body horror often focused on scientific experiments gone wrong, as in The Fly (1986), French body horror typically examined more primal, biological transformations. Baby Blood helped establish this tradition, paving the way for films like In My Skin (2002) and Trouble Every Day (2001), which explore visceral body horror through distinctly European sensibilities.
